articles.title: Penn State fans demand Matt Campbell’s job after another demoralizing loss
articles.summary: Coach Matt Campbell’s Penn State Nittany Lions are 3-3 on the season after a 31-23 home loss to Lincoln Riley’s USC Trojans that included a record-setting at...
articles.body:
Coach Matt Campbell's Penn State Nittany Lions are 3-3 on the season after a 31-23 home loss to Lincoln Riley's USC Trojans that included a record-setting attendance mark at Beaver Stadium . Campbell spoke up in favor of QB Rocco Becht after the loss but fans were far more interested in discussing the new Nittany Lions head coach's current standing with the program.

Social media was rife with thinly-veiled references to Campbell's job and whether or not he should continue in his current role. Campbell has yet to score a signature win with Penn State, and remains the target of much frustration on social media.

Fans became frustrated as Campbell's team failed to capitalize on a raucous home crowd that ranked as the fourth-largest in college football history, behind two Michigan games and a game between Tennessee and Virginia Tech in Bristol, TN in 2016.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"I genuinely never felt good about Matt Campbell…It wasn't his place like EVER to coach at Penn State," one said . "Absolutely pissed when he brought half his stupid Iowa State Cyclones team. Penn State deserves so much better man."

Another compared him to former PSU coach James Franklin.

"Campbell is a downgrade. Sucks to say but even Franklin is a better game manager and at least he can recruit. I'm honestly shocked by how bad Matt Campbell is at coaching."

"If Penn State can afford it. You fire Matt Campbell," another added. "UCLA (has) shown if the guy is correct you can compete right away in this league. Campbell was a fallback option."

"Campbell has no excuses with an easy schedule. It's a joke," another added. "Lose next week and (he's gone)." another said.

Campbell's team is going through a rough patch right now, but things will get better. The Penn State football program has the resources to bring in the talent Campbell's team needs and he should be commended for bringing Iowa State players, not criticized.

Campbell took over Penn State with a short window to get things done and to prepare for another season in a loaded Big Ten Conference, doing the best with the time he had. Becht looks like a solid option at the quarterback position and the Nittany Lions' schedule has been tougher than most people realize.

Week 5's road game at Northwestern came against a team christening a new stadium in front of 30,000 plus screaming fans and it marked one of the biggest games in the lives of NU quarterback Aidan Chiles, coach David Braun, offensive coordinator Chip Kelly and others. Fans demanded Campbell's job after the Northwestern loss , a refrain that shows little sign of slowing.

Penn State is now 0-3 in Big Ten play, an unacceptable mark considering the talent on Campbell's team. Losing to Wisconsin hurt, and losing to Northwestern made it worse. Losing to USC is forgivable, but also a painful loss as it appears to have knocked the Nittany Lions out of the Big Ten and College Football Playoff races.

Penn State doesn't have any ranked teams left on its schedule, and faces a challenging but winnable road game at Michigan in Week 7. A win over the Wolverines would go a long way toward restoring the luster on Campbell and his Penn State program. A loss would once again bring out the boo birds and the detractors as Campbell continues to find his way forward at one of the country's most recognizable college football programs.

articles.title: Liverpool v Manchester City: Toxicity and uncertainty await City at Liverpool - will their season even matter?
articles.summary: Manchester City visit Liverpool on Sunday with a lot of uncertainty hanging over them. Phil McNulty looks at what lies ahead.
articles.body:
Manchester City will face an atmosphere of toxicity and hostility they have never experienced before when they walk out to face Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

If City made a list of clubs they would prefer not to visit immediately after being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, Liverpool would be at the top ringed in red.

The relationship between the clubs has often been fractious for more than a decade, tensions fuelled by a sense of injustice felt by Liverpool fans who believe more Premier League titles should have been theirs instead of City's.

In 2013/14, 2018/19 and 2021/22, Liverpool finished second behind City – on the last two occasions by a single point - in what became, especially with Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp in charge, the defining domestic rivalry in recent years.

Liverpool supporters have long been convinced they would have won those titles had City not wielded the vast financial firepower that brought them under investigation, while those of a sky blue persuasion counter by simply highlighting the enduring brilliance and beauty of the teams Guardiola produced.

City, under new head coach Enzo Maresca, arrive at Anfield continuing to maintain their innocence after launching an appeal against the decision of an independent commission to deliver a guilty verdict.

And they arrive top of the table – but with a shadow cast over the entire season and its potential outcomes as the Premier League weighs up City's punishment, with their appeal running alongside.

As the cloud of City's guilty verdict hangs over the Premier League, each victory will carry a qualification, each league table will contain an unseen asterisk, each achievement viewed through the prism of potential future penalties and the fallout at each end of the top tier.

It has even led to the unheard of suggestion that the entire Premier League season could be rendered meaningless, given the potential scale of the consequences facing City, with talk of expulsion and relegation as well as record points deductions.

This must wait for what is likely to be a lengthy legal process, but it is against this backdrop of bitterness that City play their first league match since the verdict, in an Anfield arena that barely disguised its contempt for their fierce rivals even before that guilty verdict was handed down.

The Kop will be in no mood to await legal finalities or the outcome of an appeal. There will be sound. There will be fury. There will be resentment.

Maresca, who has not only inherited Guardiola's legacy but also the fallout from City's punishment, was calm itself in the face of a barrage of questions at his media briefing before Sunday's game.

While being at pains to point out he was present to preview a game against Liverpool , he said: "The reason I joined this club is that I completely trust, 100%, the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organisation. So I don't have doubt about that.

"It will be a tough game, for sure. We need to be ready, the focus needs to be about the game, but we know the environment at Anfield.

"It probably will be worse because of the situation but, again, it will be our duty to do our best and try to win the game. The reason I decide to become manager is for this type of game."

Maresca placed the emphasis on "when" City win their appeal, as they vehemently insist the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

The commission, in contrast, used the word "sham" eight times when describing City's dealings, including artificially inflating revenue by more than £900m through "sham" deals.

The danger now is, with sanctions and appeals to come, that this could be known in future as the "sham" Premier League season.

City have assumed their familiar position at the top of the table – but is this a title they cannot "win" with a guilty verdict hanging over them?

Former England striker Alan Shearer told BBC Radio 5 Live Sport: "I just think it's such a bad look that we're still having to wait for the consequences.

"We've never seen anything like this. This is the biggest thing to happen to the Premier League since it started in 1992, that's how big it is. Credibility matters and you won't get anything different from any coach or player at Manchester City other than we're going to stick together and we believe in the club.

"They're about to find out the anger from every club, starting at Anfield.

"It needs sorting out now because they've spent a fortune in the summer. They've won every game and that could still be the case in two months, three months, four months. They could end up winning the league. That's why it needs sorting out now because it's such a bad look if it's allowed to fester.

"The level of hostility will rise wherever they go. The ramifications are endless to this case. Where it goes after is something we don't know. It's huge. It really is massive."

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola, preparing for his first experience of this meeting of Premier League superpowers, admitted: "The worst thing probably is the uncertainty. No-one knows what's going to happen. We have to focus on Liverpool and being the best club we can be, the best team we can be. That's my challenge."

City's insistence that they will clear their name will not prevent a torrid, to put it mildly, Anfield reception.

Former Stoke City manager Tony Pulis, in his BBC Sport column , said: "I loved being the underdog and I loved to prove people wrong, and that is what I would demand now - a siege mentality from my squad and supporters alike to prove to people that, irrespective of what is happening off the pitch, on the field and the terraces we respect our club and we are going to fight on."

In what is sure to be a powder-keg atmosphere inside and outside Anfield, Merseyside Police have said there will be an "appropriate" plan in place.

This will be brought into sharper focus after incidents before a Champions League quarter-final at Anfield in April 2018, when City's team bus was attacked with bottles and flares when it arrived before the game.

Merseyside Police were unable to identify those responsible, despite viewing 130 hours of footage from the disorder, with Liverpool subsequently fined £17,500 by Uefa.

For Maresca and Manchester City 's players, shrouded in uncertainty and under threat of future Premier League punishment, Anfield – always a cauldron when they visit – will present the ultimate mental, physical and footballing examination.

articles.title: 'They beat us in every part of the game:' Austin FC routed by MLS' top team Nashville SC
articles.summary: Austin FC suffered a brutal 4-1 loss Saturday to Nashville SC in an MLS match at Q2 Stadium.
articles.body:
Austin FC picked an interesting time to have one of its most lackadaisical performances of the season.

Coming out of a two-week international break and needing a result for their ever-dwindling playoff hopes, the Verde and Black were outplayed in every aspect Saturday during a 4-1 loss to Nashville SC at Q2 Stadium.

And though Austin FC interim coach Davy Arnaud called Nashville "the best team we've played this year" and the Tennessee club currently has the best record in MLS, the Verde and Black failed to show up for most of the match, looked lethargic for long stretches and were lucky the scoreline wasn't worse.

Reed Baker-Whiting, Elias Saad, Shakur Mohammed and Hany Mukhtar scored for Nashville, while Brandon Vazquez finished Austin FC's goal.

articles.title: One Manchester City midfielder is made to thrive in the current climate
articles.summary: The Manchester City squad will have to block out the noise that currently surrounds the club. With the 115-case verdict having landed over the international...
articles.body:
The Manchester City squad will have to block out the noise that currently surrounds the club. With the 115-case verdict having landed over the international break, it has cast a heavy spotlight on the club. Despite this, the City players and staff can only control what they can control. That is matters on the pitch. It will be up to Manchester City's leaders and experienced players to lead their team through the storm. The City squad is filled with players who thrive under intense pressure. One of those is Enzo Fernandez. With everything that surrounds Manchester City, the Argentinian midfielder looks to be made to thrive in the current climate.

Enzo Fernandez is likely to embrace the situation surrounding Manchester City.

Manchester City have been cast as the villains of English football. The 115 verdict has seen City portrayed as the evil empire that has sullied the name of the Premier League. For me, that claim is laughable. But the coverage of the affair leaves no doubt about what is thought of the FA Cup and Carabao Cup holders. The City players will have to play through this lens starting today against Liverpool at Anfield. It will take incredible mental strength and fortitude for the City players to put all of that aside. They are capable of doing so. Enzo Fernandez looks to be made to thrive in the circumstances.

Enzo Fernandez is regarded as the villain of the piece. He has always been. Whether that is for Argentina or for Chelsea during his time there. Fernandez is combative, and will do whatever it takes to help his team win. His character, combined with his tremendous ability, makes him the player that he is. Playing for the 'most hated club' will not phase Enzo Fernandez. In fact, there is every possibility that he will rise to the occasion.

This trait is in his make-up and it will not shock me if Enzo Fernandez makes a stand for his team. If he can help lead the way, it will not be a surprise to see his teammates follow him. Enzo Fernandez is a leader on the pitch. Despite the fact that he has only been a Manchester City player for a short time, I'm expecting him to step up and help lead from the front.

As Enzo Maresca has pointed out, Enzo Fernandez deals with intense scrutiny playing with Argentina.

Speaking on Friday, during his pre-game press conference ahead of Manchester City's clash with Liverpool, Enzo Maresca was asked if his players could play through the pressure. The scrutiny on City is fierce right now. However, Maresca made a point of pointing out that Enzo Fernandez is used to playing in cauldron like Anfield. Maresca explained: " Absolutely they can face the pressure. Absolutely. We have players that they already experience a similar situation. I don't know, Enzo Fernandez is playing in Argentina. Argentina, it's almost every game to go to Anfield. So it's not a problem. "

Manchester City will be leaning on their leaders to guide them through the storm that surrounds the club. There will be players for Enzo Maresca's side that will rise to the occasion. One of those looks to be Enzo Fernandez. The combative midfielder is made to thrive under pressure. That is at Manchester City's door and it will not come as a surprise to see him go up a level to help his team when it matters most.

articles.title: Toxicity and uncertainty await Man City - will their season even matter?
articles.summary: Manchester City visit Liverpool on Sunday with a lot of uncertainty hanging over them. Phil McNulty looks at what lies ahead.
articles.body:
Manchester City will face an atmosphere of toxicity and hostility they have never experienced before when they walk out to face Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

If City made a list of clubs they would prefer not to visit immediately after being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, Liverpool would be at the top ringed in red.

The relationship between the clubs has often been fractious for more than a decade, tensions fuelled by a sense of injustice felt by Liverpool fans who believe more Premier League titles should have been theirs instead of City's.

In 2013/14, 2018/19 and 2021/22, Liverpool finished second behind City – on the last two occasions by a single point - in what became, especially with Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp in charge, the defining domestic rivalry in recent years.

Liverpool supporters have long been convinced they would have won those titles had City not wielded the vast financial firepower that brought them under investigation, while those of a sky blue persuasion counter by simply highlighting the enduring brilliance and beauty of the teams Guardiola produced.

City, under new head coach Enzo Maresca, arrive at Anfield continuing to maintain their innocence after launching an appeal against the decision of an independent commission to deliver a guilty verdict.

And they arrive top of the table – but with a shadow cast over the entire season and its potential outcomes as the Premier League weighs up City's punishment, with their appeal running alongside.

As the cloud of City's guilty verdict hangs over the Premier League, each victory will carry a qualification, each league table will contain an unseen asterisk, each achievement viewed through the prism of potential future penalties and the fallout at each end of the top tier.

It has even led to the unheard of suggestion that the entire Premier League season could be rendered meaningless, given the potential scale of the consequences facing City, with talk of expulsion and relegation as well as record points deductions.

This must wait for what is likely to be a lengthy legal process, but it is against this backdrop of bitterness that City play their first league match since the verdict, in an Anfield arena that barely disguised its contempt for their fierce rivals even before that guilty verdict was handed down.

The Kop will be in no mood to await legal finalities or the outcome of an appeal. There will be sound. There will be fury. There will be resentment.

Maresca, who has not only inherited Guardiola's legacy but also the fallout from City's punishment, was calm itself in the face of a barrage of questions at his media briefing before Sunday's game.

While being at pains to point out he was present to preview a game against Liverpool, he said: "The reason I joined this club is that I completely trust, 100%, the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organisation. So I don't have doubt about that.

"It will be a tough game, for sure. We need to be ready, the focus needs to be about the game, but we know the environment at Anfield.

"It probably will be worse because of the situation but, again, it will be our duty to do our best and try to win the game. The reason I decide to become manager is for this type of game."

Maresca placed the emphasis on "when" City win their appeal, as they vehemently insist the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

The commission, in contrast, used the word "sham" eight times when describing City's dealings, including artificially inflating revenue by more than £900m through "sham" deals.

The danger now is, with sanctions and appeals to come, that this could be known in future as the "sham" Premier League season.

City have assumed their familiar position at the top of the table – but is this a title they cannot "win" with a guilty verdict hanging over them?

Former England striker Alan Shearer told BBC Radio 5 Live Sport: "I just think it's such a bad look that we're still having to wait for the consequences.

"We've never seen anything like this. This is the biggest thing to happen to the Premier League since it started in 1992, that's how big it is. Credibility matters and you won't get anything different from any coach or player at Manchester City other than we're going to stick together and we believe in the club.

"They're about to find out the anger from every club, starting at Anfield.

"It needs sorting out now because they've spent a fortune in the summer. They've won every game and that could still be the case in two months, three months, four months. They could end up winning the league. That's why it needs sorting out now because it's such a bad look if it's allowed to fester.

"The level of hostility will rise wherever they go. The ramifications are endless to this case. Where it goes after is something we don't know. It's huge. It really is massive."

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola, preparing for his first experience of this meeting of Premier League superpowers, admitted: "The worst thing probably is the uncertainty. No-one knows what's going to happen. We have to focus on Liverpool and being the best club we can be, the best team we can be. That's my challenge."

City's insistence that they will clear their name will not prevent a torrid, to put it mildly, Anfield reception.

Former Stoke City manager Tony Pulis, in his BBC Sport column , said: "I loved being the underdog and I loved to prove people wrong, and that is what I would demand now - a siege mentality from my squad and supporters alike to prove to people that, irrespective of what is happening off the pitch, on the field and the terraces we respect our club and we are going to fight on."

In what is sure to be a powder-keg atmosphere inside and outside Anfield, Merseyside Police have said there will be an "appropriate" plan in place.

This will be brought into sharper focus after incidents before a Champions League quarter-final at Anfield in April 2018, when City's team bus was attacked with bottles and flares when it arrived before the game.

Merseyside Police were unable to identify those responsible, despite viewing 130 hours of footage from the disorder, with Liverpool subsequently fined £17,500 by Uefa.

For Maresca and Manchester City's players, shrouded in uncertainty and under threat of future Premier League punishment, Anfield – always a cauldron when they visit – will present the ultimate mental, physical and footballing examination.
